canonicalSemantics.summary: When knowledge of the foreign Braille system cannot be assumed, point 4 is placed before the German Braille cell of the base letter.
For exact written representation, point 4 may precede the language-specific accented Braille cell.
Point-4 announcement is required for this German-text technique in Basis-, Voll- and Kurzschrift.
The accent technique is intended for isolated foreign words or short passages within German text.
German Braille normally does not distinguish uppercase and lowercase in ordinary running text.
A document may explicitly mark all uppercase letters; in that mode unannounced letters are lowercase.
A capital letter followed by one or more lowercase letters uses the dots-4-6 marker.
An abbreviation or letter sequence beginning with one uppercase letter followed by lowercase letters uses the initial-capital marker and does not permit contractions.
A single uppercase letter or an uninterrupted uppercase sequence uses the capital-sequence marker.
Lowercase abbreviations and units without an abbreviation point, and lowercase Roman numerals, require the lowercase marker.
When more than one valid case segmentation exists, semantic grouping has priority and the number of announcement signs should then be minimized.
Greek letters in mathematical or technical contexts are announced by the Greek/foreign letter marker.
An uppercase Greek letter uses the Greek marker followed by the appropriate German uppercase announcement marker.
Case that differs from normal orthographic expectation may be explicitly represented.
Internal capitalization may be represented using the mixed-case Basisschrift method of section 2.6.4.
Customary capitalization of polite forms may optionally be carried into Braille.
When eight-dot Computerbraille inserts are not possible, Computerbraille characters are serialized through the section 2.11 six-dot transport technique.
Dot 7 is replaced by a preceding dot-4 cell while dots 1 through 6 remain in the following six-dot cell.
Dot 8 is replaced by a preceding dot-6 cell while dots 1 through 6 remain in the following six-dot cell.
Dots 7 and 8 together are replaced by a preceding dots-4-6 cell.
A Computerbraille insert whose serialized form contains no Braille blank uses the no-blank announcement marker.
A Computerbraille insert whose serialized form contains at least one Braille blank uses the blank-containing announcement marker.
The Computerbraille terminator is placed immediately after the final encoded sign, including after an encoding blank that forms part of a two-cell representation.

selectedSemantics.value: The Computerbraille terminator is placed immediately after the final encoded sign, including after an encoding blank that forms part of a two-cell representation.
The Computerbraille terminator is placed immediately after the final encoded sign, including after an encoding blank that forms part of a two-cell representation.

canonicalSemantics.summary: A single word using the first emphasis type is prefixed by the primary emphasis marker.
Blank, hyphen and slash all act as word boundaries for first-emphasis scope.
An emphasis spanning more than one word may use a multiword start marker and explicit termination after the final word.
For emphasis spanning one to three words, each word may instead be individually marked to save Braille space.
A first-emphasis word part uses the primary marker at word start and dot-6 plus the primary marker when emphasis begins inside a word.
The second emphasis type uses its alternate marker for one word and for the start of a highlighted word part.
A multiword span using the second emphasis type has a dedicated start and end sequence.
The secondary emphasis terminator may occur inside a word when only a word part is marked.
When the second emphasis spans exactly two words, each word may be marked individually to save space.
When all-capitals styling must remain recognizable as such, the span is represented in Basisschrift.
One all-capitals word is introduced by the capital-sequence marker.
A multiword all-capitals passage may use the double capital marker and explicit terminator.
An alternative emphasis technique may be used instead of explicit Versalien encoding, for example when remaining in Kurzschrift.
Foreign-language inserts may be rendered under German Basis-, Voll- or Kurzschrift.
When pronunciation is known it should be considered when selecting German Lautgruppenkürzungen for foreign text.
A foreign Braille system may be used instead of German Braille for an embedded span.
One word in a foreign Braille system is introduced by the single foreign-system marker.
A multiword foreign-system span uses a double foreign marker and explicit terminator.
The foreign alphabet or Braille system must be identified by annotation when it is not clear from context.
For foreign-system spans of one to three words, each word may be individually marked to save space.
A full foreign-system span permits the foreign system's own accented-letter signs without German point-4 accent announcement.
Mathematical signs from the section 2.10 table are normally announced with point 4 when embedded in German text.
When several mathematical signs occur in one expression, announcement of the first may remain effective through the expression.
A print letter x used as multiplication may be retained instead of replacing it with the mathematical multiplication-cross sign. The multiplication star also has an alternate text representation.
Superscripts and exponents are introduced by the exponent sign.
canonicalSemantics.integerPolicy: Positive or negative whole-number exponents use lowered digits without a number indicator.

canonicalSemantics.summary: Rear upper/lower index markers are preferably used without preceding point 4; front upper/lower index markers require point 4.
A relation is negated by prefixing dots 3-5.
When point-4 inline notation is ambiguous, the full Mathematikschrift rules and delimiters may be used to eliminate ambiguity.
The special Mathematikschrift unit indicator is normally not used in German Textschrift.
Complex mathematical expressions should switch from the inline Textschrift technique to the German Mathematikschrift system.
Arabic digits use the a-j Braille cells under one leading number indicator.
The number indicator remains effective through digits and defined decimal/grouping continuation signs; other boundaries terminate numeric scope.
Print-space grouping is normally represented by a grouping point; long identifier-like digit groups may retain spaces if the number indicator is repeated for each new group.
A leading apostrophe, leading decimal point, or dash replacing a leading zero follows the number indicator and remains part of the numeric form.
Dates and times preserve relevant print structure. A hyphen requires a new number indicator; an ambiguous textual colon is announced before the next numeric component.
For simple natural-number fractions, the numerator uses cardinal digits and the denominator is appended using lowered digits without its own number indicator.
canonicalSemantics.mixedFractionPolicy: A mixed-number fractional component is attached without a space but begins with its own number indicator.

canonicalSemantics.summary: Specially formed letter-like symbols use point 4 before the corresponding letter cell.
A dash between or inside numbers has no surrounding blank and the number indicator must be repeated for the following number.
The text slash may occur between numeric components; the following numeric component re-enters numeric state.
